q7.answer: The API generates 32 random bytes in step 2, before the transaction, and encodes them as URL-safe text. That raw token goes into the email link and into the email job payload, and only its SHA-256 hash is written to password_reset_tokens.

q8.answer: On page load, the API hashes the t parameter and looks up the row by token_hash, then checks used_at, invalidated_at and expires_at; the form is shown only if all pass, and loading writes nothing. On POST, the same checks run again inside the transaction under row locks, and that submit-time check is the one that decides the reset.

q9.answer: There is no separate counter: the count is a query over password_reset_tokens rows for that user_id with created_at in the last hour, including used and invalidated rows. Old requests drop out of the count automatically as their created_at passes one hour, so the periodic purge is not needed for correctness; how the purge is scheduled is still open.

q10.answer: In the forgot-password transaction, after the user row lock and the count check pass, every earlier row for the account with used_at and invalidated_at both NULL is set to invalidated_at = now(), before the new row is inserted. Requests refused by the limit never reach this step, so they cannot invalidate an earlier link.

q11.answer: In one transaction, the reset updates users.password_hash, sets used_at on the token row, and deletes all of the user's sessions rows. After COMMIT, the 'your password was changed' email is queued, and then the response is a 302 to /login with no session created.

q12.answer: Both flows lock the users row first and then the token row with FOR UPDATE, so the requests are serialized in one order and cannot deadlock. The second submit waits on the token lock, then sees used_at set and gets the expired page, so exactly one password change can commit per token.
